A learned society founded in Calcutta on 15 January 1784 by the British judge and linguist William Jones, to study the history, languages, science and culture of Asia. It still exists in Kolkata.

The governor-general Warren Hastings backed it. Its journal, Asiatick Researches, brought Indian learning to European readers. Members translated Sanskrit classics such as Kalidasa's play Shakuntala and the law book of Manu.

In 1786 Jones gave his famous address noting that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were so alike that they must spring from a common source, now lost. The idea launched comparative linguistics and the concept of the Indo-European language family, traced back today to Proto-Indo-European.

The society's scholars also recovered India's own forgotten past. In 1837 its secretary James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script and read the Edicts of Ashoka, restoring the emperor to history. The society was a product of East India Company rule, and its knowledge also served that rule, but it laid the base of modern Indian studies.
